name: Obolo
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Faraclas, Nicholas. 1984. Tone and phrase stress: The extra high tone in Obolo. Journal of West African Languages 14(1): 3-17.
catalog_locator: pp. 4-5 (section 1 'Phrase stress in Obolo') and p. 9; further pp. 10-13 (automatically stressed morphemes, stress spreading, suspension of non-initial phrase stress, lexical extra high). Scan has; page = scan page + 2.
catalog_quote: In Obolo, each syllable of a noun is assigned one tone lexically, while each verb stem is assigned a single tone (high or low) which is distributed suprasegmentally over however many syllables it may contain. The systems of lexical tone and downdrift, however, coexist and interact with other suprasegmental systems, including a system of phrasal stress. [p. 4] ... In Obolo, the speech chain divides itself into several units of varying length which correspond to the different units to which suprasegmental features are assigned. Intonation patterns are realized over pause groups, which are usually bounded by pauses before and after, as the name would suggest. Phrase stress is realized over stress groups, which are usually smaller than pause groups (although the two may coincide over one single phrase). One phrase stress is assigned to each stress group in a given utterance. [p. 5] ... While the criteria which determine the boundaries of stress groups are purely syntactic, the criteria that enter into the determination of which syllable within each stress group will actually carry the stress are not only morphosyntactic, but phonological and semantic-pragmatic as well. [p. 9]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Obolo (obol1243) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title lists two stress-titled works, both Faraclas 1984. (1) JWAL 14(1) 'Tone and phrase stress: the extra high tone in Obolo' was already held by the project from the earlier reading today (open JWAL archive PDF + 300-dpi scanned) and was read in full: it is the first-hand, instrumentally backed description of Obolo suprasegmentals — three tonemes plus a phrase-stress system with one stress per syntactic stress group, placed by ranked phonological/morphosyntactic/pragmatic criteria, with extra-high-toned grammatical morphemes automatically stressed; no word-stress rule exists. (2) JALL 6(2) 'Tone, stress, and the Obolo verbal focus system' (doi 10.1515/jall.1984.6.2.127) is closed everywhere checked (Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, CrossRef; de Gruyter/Brill page WAF-blocked; not on archive.org/CORE; HathiTrust could not be reached by automated download) — medium priority, expected to be the phrase-stress/focus application rather than a word-stress statement. Also held by the project and consistent: Faraclas 1982 JWAL 12(2): 77 (primary sentence stress on one syllable per rhythm group) and Connell 1994 JWAL 24(1): 12 (only Faraclas 1984 has investigated phrasal stress in Lower Cross). Not obtainable: Faraclas 1984 'A grammar of Obolo' (IULC; CORE/MPG.PuRe record only, no text), Faraclas 'A phonology of the western dialects of Obolo' (cited as forthcoming; fn. 1 says its ch. 6-7 hold the stress/tone material; no published record), Rowland-Oke 2003 (Google Books feed gives blurb only; New web records appended to under a dated addendum. Recommended catalog entry: tone language, phrase-level stress only, no word stress; deciding source Faraclas 1984 JWAL pp. 4-5, 9-11.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Obolo is a tone language (three tonemes: high, low, extra high; nouns carry a tone per syllable, verb stems a single H or L). Stress exists only at the phrase level: each syntactically defined 'stress group' (a verb phrase with its arguments, an adverbial complement, or a detached noun phrase; each serial verb and indirect object is its own group) receives exactly one phrase stress, cued by extra-high pitch, higher amplitude and extra length. Which syllable within the group carries it is not fixed by word position: stress gravitates to underlyingly non-low syllables and group boundaries (phonological), to extra-high-toned verbal prefixes, the first morpheme of a place/time/manner complement, extra-high verb roots and prominent subject NPs (morphosyntactic), and follows verb-focus patterns (semantic-pragmatic). Certain extra-high-toned grammatical morphemes (negative ka, future ma/mo/me, 3sg completive i, question words, interjections, imperatives) are automatically stressed. No word-level stress rule is given.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Faraclas 1984 p. 11: 'In some cases, the stress seems to distribute itself evenly over two or even three syllables'; Faraclas 1982 p. 77: 'Primary sentence stress is usually assigned to one syllable of this [rhythm] group. Serialized verbs and indirect object phrases.. as well as complements of time, manner, or location tend to detach themselves from the rest of the sentence, receiving secondary stress in most cases.'
new_statements.exceptions: Under information-question, imperative, negative, exclamatory, hypothetical and indirect-discourse intonation only the first stress group of a pause group receives phrase stress (p. 11-12). Extra high tone on noun stems occurs 'in cases where there is no apparent reason to postulate accent or stress at any level' (p. 13), i.e. lexical extra high is not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phrase ('stress group'), not the word; data are connected speech and read sentences with F0 measurements from the University of Ibadan phonetics lab. Language is tonal, so the secondary reading 'tone language with a stress statement' also applies. Vowel-length table (p. 5) shows stressed vowels ~215-245 ms vs unstressed 118-181 ms. Analysis is of the Western dialects.
new_statements.identity_note: Faraclas's data are explicitly from the "Western dialects of Obolo" (title of Faraclas 1982; fn. 1 of Faraclas 1984 says the material comes from his "A Phonology of the Western Dialects of Obolo", to appear). Connell 2016 (SPiL Plus 48: 11) notes Faraclas 1984 is based on one dialect and that eastern coastal varieties remain undocumented. Glottolog 5.3 lists no dialect-level languoids under obol1243, so no dialect glottocode can be given.

tone_statements.quote: Our analysis relies entirely on Faraclas (1984, 122 pages). Obolo distinguishes an extra high (circumflex accent), a high (acute accent), and a low tone (unmarked)1. The tonal shape of some verb forms is the sum of the tones of the SM, any AM marker, and the tone of the root, but in many forms there is a superimposed tonal shape so that the tonal contour is not the sum of the tones of individual morphemes. Tone is very important in verbal distinctions. ... [fn. 1] Faraclas says each of the three has two major allotones ... so we simply refer to the three tones as extra high, high, and low.
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones (extra high, high, low) after Faraclas 1984, each with a level and a gliding allotone; verb forms carry superimposed tonal shapes; stress is phrasal, marked by extra-high or glide.

sources.note: Obolo has three tonemes (H, L, extra high) plus a system of phrase stress: one phrase stress per syntactically defined stress group (verb phrase, adverbial complement, detached NP); cues are extra-high F0, amplitude, length; which syllable in the group is stressed follows phonological > morphosyntactic > semantic-pragmatic hierarchies; some extra-high-toned grammatical morphemes (negative ka, future ma/mo/me, 3sg completive, question words) are automatically stressed; stress may spread over 2-3 syllables; no word-level stress rule is given (pp. 4-5, 9-11).

sources.note: p. 77: 'Preliminary stress and intonation studies indicate that, in Obolo statement intonation, the speech chain divides itself into rhythm groups centered either around a verb or around a complement of time, location, or manner.. Primary sentence stress is usually assigned to one syllable of this group. Serialized verbs and indirect object phrases.. as well as complements of time, manner, or location tend to detach themselves from the rest of the sentence, receiving secondary stress in most cases.'
